analysis.one_liner: Requires health plans to cover hospital stays as long as the attending doctor and patient decide is needed.
analysis.headline: The bill never left its Senate committee and died when the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999, without a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require group and individual health insurance, employer plans, Medicare private plans, Medicaid managed care, and Medigap policies to cover a hospital stay for as long as the attending doctor, consulting the patient, judges medically appropriate. Insurers could not require doctors to get advance approval for the stay length, could not pay patients rebates to leave early, and could not penalize doctors who kept patients longer. It would take effect for plan years starting January 1, 1999.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients facing pressure to leave the hospital before they feel ready. The bill lets the doctor at the bedside—not the insurance plan—set how long a hospital stay lasts, and forbids plans from paying patients to leave early or cutting a doctor's pay for keeping a patient longer.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Hospital patients, especially new mothers and older adults

how_it_helps.text: Requires group and individual health plans to cover a hospital stay for the length the attending physician, in consultation with the patient, determines medically appropriate, and bars plans from requiring pre-authorization for that length of stay.

Prohibits insurers from offering patients money or rebates to accept less than these protections, from penalizing providers who follow the rule, and from making later portions of a covered stay less favorable than earlier portions.

Extends the same protections to Medicare beneficiaries in private plans, Medigap policyholders, and Medicaid beneficiaries enrolled in managed care, and lets state laws with stronger patient protections stand instead of the federal floor.
Lets patients leave when they choose—the bill creates no fixed minimum stay for any procedure.

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and managed care plans, which would cover longer hospital stays and lose their authority to cap them; premiums for employers and policyholders could rise as a result.
analysis.who_pays_short: Health insurers and managed care plans

drawbacks.text: Insurers and employers would bear the cost of longer covered stays, and the bill explicitly preserves plans' ability to pass cost-sharing like deductibles and coinsurance to patients, so some of the cost could reach premiums and out-of-pocket payments.

Critics of coverage mandates argued that giving the attending provider unilateral control over stay length, without any plan review, removes a cost-control check and could encourage unnecessarily long stays; the bill allows plans to negotiate reimbursement levels but not to second-guess the length itself.

The bill leaves the decision in one doctor's hands in consultation with the patient, which supporters intended as patient protection but which gives plans no role in review even when utilization might reasonably be questioned.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For patients, the benefit is direct: no one gets pushed out of a hospital bed by an insurer's clock. The real cost is money—longer stays mean higher claims, and some of that lands on premiums and cost-sharing, which hits working families too. A reasonable middle path (for example, allowing quick plan review of very long stays) is absent; the bill drew the line entirely on the doctor's side. Still, this was a narrow mandate in the same family as the 1996 law requiring minimum stays after childbirth, not a sweeping restructuring.

outcome.mechanism: It was read twice and referred to the Senate Labor and Human Resources Committee in July 1998, the committee never acted on it, and it died when the Congress ended in January 1999.

narrative.text: Sen. Dianne Feinstein introduced the bill on July 15, 1998, with Sen. Alfonse D'Amato and Sen. Wendell Ford joining, giving it two Democrats and one Republican behind it.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Labor and Human Resources on the day it was introduced.
No further action appears in the record: the committee never held a markup or reported the bill, and the full Senate never voted on it before the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and managed care plans kept their authority to limit hospital stays, since no competing law filled the gap before the Congress ended.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Health insurers and managed care plans

sides.party_line_note: The bill was bipartisan from the start—two Democrats and one Republican—but no votes were ever taken, so the partisan shape of any opposition is unknown.

industries.industry: Health insurers and managed care plans
industries.note: The bill strips plans of their authority to cap hospital stays and to require pre-authorization for a doctor's chosen length of stay, and bars them from paying patients to leave early or incentivizing doctors to discharge sooner. That discretion is a core cost-control tool for the industry.

Longer covered stays mean more inpatient revenue for hospitals, and the bill's rules against reimbursing doctors less for keeping patients longer reinforce that. Patients could also benefit from not being discharged before they are ready.
The bill makes compliance with the doctor-determined stay standard a condition for Medicare+Choice contracts and Medigap certification, extending the mandate to plans serving seniors.
